scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

Based on the scenario, I’d say your approach leans **toward a 0/1 (unfair or wrong)**, but with important context to consider. Here’s why: ### **Why This Feels Problematic (0/1)** 1. **Prioritizing Family Over Partnership Without Compromise** - You’ve been together for **three years**, and while she’s been working hard to support herself, you’ve been prioritizing family needs (emotionally, financially, and time-wise) over building a shared future. That’s a **fundamental imbalance** in a relationship where trust and commitment are supposed to be reciprocal. - She’s not asking you to **abandon** your family—she’s asking for **equality in effort**. Right now, she’s the one carrying the financial burden (student loans, rent, school fees) while you’re focused on family obligations. That’s not sustainable for a long-term partnership. 2. **Her Feelings Matter** - She’s **not asking for money**—she’s asking for **your time, focus, and shared goals**. When she says she feels like you’ll "never care enough" about *her* future, that’s a **valid concern**. If you truly love her, you’d want to see her thrive, not just survive. - Her sadness and frustration aren’t irrational. She’s been **prioritizing herself** (studying, working, saving) while you’ve been prioritizing others. That’s a **double standard** that will erode trust over time. 3. **The "Family Always Comes First" Mindset Can Be Harmful** - While family loyalty is important, **absolute prioritization** (especially when it comes at the expense of your own life and partner’s happiness) can create resentment. Many people in long-term relationships struggle with this—balancing family, career, and partnership is key. - If you **never** make time for her dreams (like saving for a house together), she’ll eventually feel like she’s **second to everyone else**, including your future self. --- ### **Why There’s Some Understanding (But Not Excuse)** - **Your Family’s Needs Are Real** – You’re not wrong for wanting to support them, but **how you communicate it matters**. Saying "family always comes first" without acknowledging her feelings is dismissive. - **She’s Not Asking You to Cut Ties** – She’s asking for **shared goals**. A future where you both save, plan, and grow together isn’t about abandoning family—it’s about **not neglecting your own life and hers**. - **You’re Both Young & Struggling Financially** – This is a **common struggle** for young couples, but it’s not an excuse to ignore the relationship’s foundation. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead (A Better Approach)** 1. **Acknowledge Her Feelings First** - Instead of saying *"Family always comes first,"* try: *"I love you, and I want us to have a future together. But I also feel guilty when I don’t spend time with my family because they’ve been there for me. I want to figure out a way to balance both—maybe we can set small goals together?"* - This shows **empathy** while still honoring your values. 2. **Set Shared Priorities (Not Just Yours)** - Instead of saying *"I’ll help family first,"* say: *"I want us to save for a house together after I finish my real estate license. Can we start small—like putting aside $200/month each?"* - This makes her feel **included** in the plan, not left out. 3. **Reassess Family Expectations** - If your family **demands** constant attention, can you set boundaries? (e.g., *"I’ll be there for big events, but I need time to focus on us too."*) - If they’re **financially stable** (like your mom’s settlement), maybe some of your help can shift to **emotional support** rather than financial. 4. **Show Action, Not Just Words** - She’s not asking for perfection—she’s asking for **effort**. If you **start studying for your license** (even just 1 hour a day) and **save a little together**, that will show her you’re serious. --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not Wrong for Caring About Family… But You’re Wrong for Not Balancing It** - **0/1 (Unfair/Wrong)** because your current approach **prioritizes family over her** without considering her needs. - **But** you’re not a bad person—you just need to **reframe how you communicate and act**. **The key question:** *Can you love her enough to also love your future with her?* If the answer is yes, then **adjust your priorities**—not abandon them, but **include her in them**. Would you say you’re open to trying a more balanced approach? Because if you both work on it, you *can* have a strong family bond **and** a strong future together. 💛
